title: Looking Back on My Days in Gdansk
paragraphs: Hello everyone. From spring to summer 2013, for about three months, I studied abroad at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. This time I would like to introduce that experience.

Let me begin by introducing Poland and Gdansk. Poland is an agricultural country whose land is mostly plains. Ethnically it is Slavic, and its native Polish is close to Russian, but religiously it is Catholic. The Kingdom of Poland boasted vast territory from the Middle Ages to the 17th century, but from the 18th century on it was tossed about among the surrounding great powers and vanished from the map several times, and after the Second World War it became part of the communist bloc, so a long period of hardship continued. Today, after democratization, it has joined the EU and is developing economically at a remarkable pace, but on the other hand it also has many difficult problems, such as contradictions between old systems and new mechanisms and economic disparities.

Gdansk is a port city on the Baltic Sea in the north, open since ancient times, which once flourished as an autonomous city belonging to the Hanseatic League, and in the 20th century, because of its importance as a strategic point, it also became the place where the Second World War broke out. In the fierce fighting at that time, most of the beautiful old town that had continued since the Middle Ages was destroyed, but after the war quite rigorous restoration was undertaken, and today it has regained an old-world appearance of which, if you did not know, you would not realize that it is a reconstruction.

Now, the Medical University of Gdansk, within walking distance of that lovely old town of Gdansk, has, in addition to the regular course that educates Poles in Polish, a six-year course that accepts students from overseas and teaches in English. This time I took part mainly in a part of this course. In this course, students spend two years, the fifth and sixth, doing what in Japan is called polyclinic clerkships. The content is also similar to Japan, with group lectures, small-group lectures while going around the wards and laboratories, and practice in procedures and examinations. The course lectures were mainly systematic ones following EU guidelines, and some were a review of what I had learned in Japan (and English study?), but there were also many differences in culture, systems and ways of thinking about diseases, so I was able to learn with a fresh feeling. The students in this course are most often from the Nordic countries, which are geographically close, and there are also students from English-speaking countries and various European countries. Among the sixth-year students nearing graduation in particular, there were many excellent people, and I was impressed and stimulated by their remarks in lectures and clerkships.

In medical care at the university hospital, EU guidelines are quite widespread, and for example I felt that the flow of treatment of a patient brought in on suspicion of myocardial infarction was not very different from Japan and other developed countries. On the other hand, I also saw and heard of many circumstances specific to this country, such as drugs that are the first choice in other EU countries being unapproved and unavailable for some diseases, and long waiting lists for admission to the university hospital.

Each department was one or two weeks, and I actively chose departments that are not very major in Japan, such as family medicine, medical oncology and rheumatology. I had imagined that rheumatology would be the same as collagen disease medicine, but here it handles a quite wide range of diseases, including metabolic diseases such as gout and orthopedic diseases such as osteoarthritis. In the clerkship, what impressed me was that they perform detailed orthopedic-style physical examinations for various collagen diseases and put effort into the medical prevention of gout and osteoarthritis. Medical oncology is a young department that was institutionalized only a few years ago. On the ward there were patients with a wide range of cancers, from lung cancer to lymphoma, brain tumors and gynecological cancers. At this university treatment rather than diagnosis is the focus, and the work centered on chemotherapy and radiation therapy and temporary management of patients whose general condition had deteriorated.

On the last day of the clerkship in many departments there was an exam, and I took it together with the regular students. The questions are mostly drawn from what was learned during the clerkship, but even things I knew in Japanese faced a language hurdle, so from the middle of each clerkship I was chased by exam preparation. It was unclear how my grades during the study abroad would be recognized if I failed, so I took them on pins and needles, but fortunately I passed all of them and breathed a sigh of relief.

Unfortunately, during the course there are not many opportunities to perform procedures or examinations on real patients. A major reason is that the patients speak only the local language. However, for the latter one month of the study abroad period, because the local summer vacation had begun, I did not take part in the course but followed teachers in the departments of my choice individually, and then I could accompany actual ward work and rounds, and sometimes (with an interpreter!) was given the opportunity to do medical interviews and physical examinations.

In taking part in the course in the first half, the curriculum was properly organized and there were many classmates, so I was able to experience student life overseas and the atmosphere of medical education. And in the individual clerkship in the second half, I learned about the state of the wards and how doctors work, and as a result I think it was very good to be able to know both the clinical and the educational sides.

From here on, please let me write a little about life and culture there. Where I stayed was a student dormitory about ten minutes' walk from the university and the hospital. It was on a site cut into a mountain slope, with a forest spreading behind the dormitory, and during my stay, walking in the forest in the evening was very pleasant and something to look forward to. The rooms were simply built and the facilities were shared. For daily meals, I ate lunch in the hospital cafeteria, and otherwise I bought cooking utensils, shopped at local supermarkets and cooked for myself. I knew almost nothing about Polish cuisine before studying abroad, but although it does not have the sophistication of court cuisine, the ingredients and cooking methods are varied (especially meat dishes and soups come in great variety), and there were many dishes that suited my Japanese palate, so in this respect it pleasantly betrayed my expectations (although there were several times when the portions of meat dishes were so large that I was at a loss for words).

Toward the Polish people I had an impression of somehow simplicity and nostalgia. There were many kind people, and when I asked something, or with the people I got to know through chance, they were very sincere.

Thank you for reading. I would be happy if this account has made you a little interested in Poland. Looking back on the three months, I think that thanks to the help of various people I was able to do a meaningful clerkship. I thank everyone who looked after me. Thank you very much!
